name: Nora Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. What you say is confidential; you can give me the public line and your private view. What does a usual working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Nora, 27, and I lead a team that maintains ticketing software for a tech company. My master's gave me a good base, but most mornings begin with a passenger's failed scan or a disputed charge; I enjoy making the chain of events legible before we release a fix. The tedious part is explaining why a neat-looking summary missed the one card that was charged twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've found another useful tool for the small jobs, and that's about it. I sometimes use an assistant to turn a long fault log into a short list, but I check the list against the actual failed ticket scans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job and pay feel steady under this picture. I earn well as the lead on our ticketing software, have eight months of living costs saved, and there are many software teams around here; a delayed release bothers me more than AI hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the morning incident review and the weekly release sign-off. In the first year I'd try the log summary on one older incident at a time, with no customer details, and keep adding 200 to my savings each payday while the pay stays good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd rather spend an hour fixing a passenger's double charge than admiring an AI summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the summary miss something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday the summary missed a repeated card charge because the messages looked different. I spotted it only by lining up the timestamps, which is why the tool gets a check, not a signature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money you keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older brother says I should buy a better car with my salary. The current car starts every morning, so I'd rather keep the cash where I can use it if work changes.

say: I'd call the **log summary** useful when a person checks it against ticket scans.
I'd say small savings in time leave the **release sign-off** with us.
think: I feel secure with **eight months saved**, higher pay and many nearby software teams.
I worry more about **duplicate charges** than a mild AI change.
do: Keep the **morning incident review** and weekly sign-off.
Try log summaries on **older incidents** without customer details.
Add **200 each payday** to savings while pay stays good.
feel: **Calm** and focused on customer billing faults.
S0.quote: I'd rather spend an hour fixing a passenger's double charge than admiring an AI summary.
fieldNote: **Eight months saved** and plenty of local jobs make her current work and income feel secure.
She uses AI occasionally, but a missed **duplicate charge** keeps her attached to timestamp checks.

steps.text: Run morning incident reviews and sign weekly software releases
Try an AI log summary on old incidents without customer details
Add 200 to savings each payday while pay stays good

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my colleagues that writing code and answering support tickets are the first places we'd see fewer hands at keyboards. We should count missed charges as carefully as time saved before changing the release team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could probably keep a lead role for a while, but if the firm needs half as many developers, I can't assume I'm in the surviving half. Eight months saved makes a search possible, and there are other employers nearby, yet the work itself would be changing across all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a three-month pilot on old incidents and compare missed charges, fix times and hours spent checking AI output. During the first year of the shift I'd learn the firm's new review process only after the pilot shows it works, and I'd avoid taking on a bigger car loan until I know whether my salary holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at first, then anxious when I picture the same cuts at several firms. I can adjust, but I don't control how many posts remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What belongs in the pilot beyond speed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A missed charge is not just a score on a chart; someone has to refund the passenger and explain it. I'd ask the support desk to tell us what happened after each bad release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot shows a serious error?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the pilot found more missed charges, I'd argue to keep manual sign-off on that part of the system. I wouldn't claim the whole tool is useless just because one part failed.

say: I'd ask colleagues to count **missed charges** alongside hours saved.
I'd say **support replies** and code writing could need fewer people.
think: I may lose **lead pay** if firms reduce developer posts widely.
My **eight-month cushion** buys search time, though nearby firms may face similar cuts.
do: Run a **three-month pilot** on old incidents with error and review-time measures.
Learn the **new review process** only if pilot results support it.
Delay a **car loan** until I know whether salary holds.
feel: **Anxious** about cuts across firms, despite savings and options.
S1.quote: A missed charge is not just a score on a chart; someone has to refund the passenger and explain it.
fieldNote: **Strong savings** soften her personal risk but cannot guarantee another software post if several firms cut staff.
She takes a **measured approach**, and her pilot includes customer harm as well as speed.

steps.text: Pilot AI incident review on old cases for three months
Learn revised release review only if pilot results show it works
Delay a larger car loan until salary prospects are clear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 would reach our ticketing code long before hands-on robots arrive around 2031. People deserve to know who handles refunds when machines make a bad charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose my lead post even if I'm good at it, because designing and checking software is exactly the thinking work the card describes. My eight months of savings and the number of local firms buy me time, but if everyone changes hiring together, the options may thin quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep leading weekly ticketing releases while putting work samples and incident records in order without customer data, and ask three local firms what paid reliability work they still expect to need. If my job ended in the first year after 2028, I'd apply to those posts only when they exist, and spend from savings while looking rather than accept a role that cannot cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not lost. I can afford a search, but I cannot guarantee what the search will find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner what the savings are for. My eight months of savings are for rent and food, not a holiday or a gamble on stocks. We'd keep the present flat until one of us had a firm offer that made a move sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would a work sample show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work sample would show the double-charge fix and how we found it, but no passenger names or card numbers. I want an employer to see the judgment, not a copied database.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** reaches our code before 2031 robots matter.
I'd ask who is **paid to handle refunds** after an automated mistake.
think: I could lose my **lead post** even with strong skill.
I have **eight months' expenses**, but local hiring could shrink across firms.
do: Keep **leading releases** while preparing incident samples without customer data now.
Ask **three local firms** now; apply after a cut only to real posts whose wages cover rent.
Keep the **current flat** until a firm offer makes moving sensible.
feel: **Anxious**, but able to fund a careful job search.
S2.quote: My eight months of savings are for rent and food, not a holiday or a gamble on stocks.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** strikes her design and checking work in 2028; later robots offer no delay.
She has **search time** but tests paid vacancies, and protects customer data in her work samples.

steps.text: Keep leading ticketing releases while preparing incident samples without customer data
Apply to existing paid reliability posts after a cut only if wages cover rent
Keep current flat until a firm offer makes moving sensible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to 2031 lets us test the system in public-facing work before rebuilding a team around it. Robots arriving around 2034 are a different timetable from the thinking AI that reaches our code first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to make a living checking who is accountable for faulty ticket charges, but that depends on someone paying for that responsibility. The time lets me learn from proven tools and build a wider savings buffer without rushing into a job title that exists only on a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the support manager to let me spend one day a month tracing disputed charges end to end, if my current manager agrees to release the time. I'd take a short course in payment security only if my firm pays the fee; in the first year after 2031 I'd apply for paid payment-review work if our own team is reduced and those jobs actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can picture a route. Five years makes room for the course and a real record of disputes, not just hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during a support-day visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The support manager would need to show me the refund process, including who calls the passenger. If my manager cannot spare a day a month, I would keep the weekly sign-off and try again next quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is not funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for an expensive course myself while the job still pays well; I can learn some of the basics from our incident manual first. A funded payment security course is a real offer.

say: I'd say **2031 thinking AI** reaches code before 2034 robots.
I'd ask for **real refund records** before redesigning a release team.
think: I might earn from **payment review** if firms pay for human accountability.
I need **proven tools** and paid work, not just a new title.
do: Learn the **refund process** through monthly disputed-charge reviews if both managers release the time.
Take **payment security training** only if my firm pays the fee.
Apply after 2031 for **paid review work** only if our team shrinks and posts exist.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to test a plausible route.
S3.quote: A funded payment security course is a real offer.
fieldNote: **Five years** let her test support-side review with both managers' agreement and a funded course.
She treats **paid review demand** as uncertain and will apply only if her team contracts and real posts appear.

steps.text: Trace disputed charges monthly if both managers release the time
Take payment security course only if the firm pays
Apply for paid payment-review posts after 2031 only if team shrinks and vacancies exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team ten years before 2036 gives us time to keep the ticketing rules understandable, even if code itself becomes cheap. Thinking AI comes before the 2039 robots, so software teams can't wait for the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could reach 37 with enough savings to choose a smaller role or a different employer, but that only holds if my pay continues and I keep expenses sensible. I don't see a reason to leave a good job today because of a forecast ten years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep documenting the refund decisions behind each release and make the incident guide usable by the support desk. I'd add 200 to savings on pay day while my salary holds, and if payment-review work still pays in the first year after 2036, I'd compare firm offers and move only for better paid payment-review work; otherwise I'd stay in whichever paid role I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years. I know a decade is not a promise, but I have enough room to revise plans as evidence arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guide say about a refund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guide would say which charges require a person to approve a refund and what a customer should hear. I don't want refund rules locked in my head or a tool no one can question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade change your housing plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I could move to a larger place one day, but I'd want the rent covered on our wages as they are, not on an imagined future salary. For now the current flat works.

say: I'd say **2036 thinking AI** reaches code before 2039 robots.
I'd ask the team to keep **refund rules** readable for support staff.
think: I could have **more choices** at 37 if my pay and savings hold.
I see no need to leave a **good paid job** today on a forecast.
do: Document **refund decisions** in a support guide through the decade.
Add **200 on pay day** to savings while salary holds.
Compare **firm offers** after 2036 and move only for better paid payment-review work.
feel: **Calm** about the next few years, with room to revise plans.
S4.quote: I don't want refund rules locked in my head or a tool no one can question.
fieldNote: **High pay**, eight months saved and many local employers support present calm even with a distant AGI date.
She preserves **refund knowledge** and makes later job moves depend on actual paid offers.

steps.text: Document refund approval rules in a guide for support staff
Add 200 to savings each payday while salary holds
Move to payment review after 2036 only for a better paid firm offer

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our design and checks change before we can test the replacement properly. Clear paid roles, time to verify refunds and a real notice period would help me use my savings for a search instead of a scramble.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a passenger learns a charge was wrong. A refund needs a reason someone can explain, not a tidy code change that no one understands.

headlineQuote: A refund needs a reason someone can explain, not a tidy code change that no one understands.
portrait: Nora, **27**, leads a tech company's ticketing software team after a master's degree and checks disputed charges against real scans.
Her **higher pay**, eight months saved and many nearby employers make current work and money feel secure.
She uses AI **occasionally** for logs but checks timestamps after a summary missed a double charge.
Steady disruption makes her **anxious** about broad staffing cuts; fast AGI threatens code and review work directly.
With more time, she would test **payment review**, take funded training and keep refund rules clear for support staff.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut software roles before employers prove who will check and explain wrong charges.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear paid roles**, refund-checking time and real notice would let her search carefully.
